root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: TheSump makes settling a cold tar basin a struggle over ordinary actions: moving, working, staying clean and getting back what the black has kept. A colony learns to read its mice and plants, chooses routes through sticky ground, and turns the same troublesome tar into useful materials, beautiful gaslight and a pantry that preserves at the price of solvent. Digging buys a chance at deep-time finds while risking a preserved trap or something much larger below. Channels and gates let the colony put tar to work, but a belch or a careless burn can change the ground it thought it understood. An ordinarily woken tar beast is a catastrophe to evacuate ahead of; deliberately pouring solvent wakes a different danger that hunts the map. The tools make a messy settlement possible without making the Sump surrender.

Sources: design/RimMandrake/biome_experiences_2026-10-20.md; design/Jawa/worldbuilding/biomes/sump_flora_roster_2026-09-24.md; src/RimMandrake/EnvironmentalHazards/Source/RM_MapComponent_SumpLivingMap.cs.

F2: Resistance becomes empty punishment: the colony cleans and trudges without meaningful finds, warm light, preservation or useful control of tar; the opposite false success makes the place surrender once a floor is built. Sources: infrastructure/state/items/SUMP_INHABITED_NOTES_1.md; infrastructure/state/items/SUMP_GASLIGHT_1.md; infrastructure/state/items/closed/SUMP_TAR_VAULT_1.md.

F3: Colony-scale coping fails or silently changes: vault recovery re-seals food, settings strand preservation, a burn outruns its firebreak, or a giant's evacuation offers no useful decision. A neat direct-method proof still passes. asks.title: The ordinary moment — ASK FIRST
asks.picture: A worker carries lunch across black ground, brings tar indoors, and gets the useful find home only after another awkward journey. That evening the same colony sits beside a lamp made from tar and acid.
asks.text: Which ordinary moment makes that your Sump, and where does the proposed root give you the wrong picture?
asks.why: F1/F2. A catalogue of hazards can miss your sentence's force: even an ordinary errand must feel like dealing with this place.
asks.guess: The everyday struggle comes first, with clever use of the same tar making life possible. I recommend that as the root's centre.
asks.tree_change: If everyday resistance leads, root acceptance follows a complete working day. If reading hidden danger leads, lead with a careful expedition and its decisions. If making use of tar leads, lead with production and preservation. All existing capabilities retain coverage; a correction rewrites dependent claims. No answer approves a root.
asks.decision: Root emphasis and its ordinary-play rejection case.
asks.author: Codex Designer dry run, 2026-11-10
asks.speaker: agent
asks.review_status: Local evidence/wording check only; independent author review pending; not sent.

asks.title: The first demonstration — ASK FIRST
asks.picture: A: a first expedition reads the mice, works a shaft, and hears the click. B: forty colonists keep food, routes and lamps working through a normal dirty day. C: a defended station operates its tar channels and firebreaks, then evacuates ahead of the ordinary station-eating beast. These are three scene drafts, not captures or accepted demonstrations.
asks.text: Which scene goes first when you decide whether we understood the Sump, and what failure there would stop you?
asks.why: F1–F3. No flagship pick was found. A spectacular fire could hide an empty daily life; a tidy little test could hide a colony that cannot cope.
asks.guess: B first: your experience sentence is about every action. A follows to test the hidden dangers, then C for consequences at a larger scale.
asks.tree_change: A selects expedition as showcase 1; B selects ordinary colony life; C selects station emergency. The actual owner pick must later be recorded separately from root approval. Other independent capabilities keep their scenes; later showcases must add different functionality.
asks.decision: Owner's flagship scene and its immediate reject case.

asks.title: A settlement that knows what it is doing
asks.picture: The colony now has forty people, glass routes, stocked solvent, a pantry and dependable lamps. The player has learned the place and supplied the coping tools. Tar still comes home from outside work.
asks.text: What still takes your attention on an ordinary day here, and what should the colony now manage for itself?
asks.why: F2/F3. Your dirty-colony rule and generous local solvent are settled. The unresolved bar is whether mature play means recurring decisions or repeatedly issuing the same cleaning and retrieval orders.
asks.guess: I still choose routes, work sites and where to spend effort; stocked routine cleaning and food handling run through ordinary colony work. The colony stays dirty without constant repeated clicks.
asks.tree_change: If routine care should run itself, require repeatable ordinary jobs and stock/solvent controls at colony scale. If hands-on extraction is part of play, require useful batch orders and an explicit amount of attention. If only special emergencies need attention, tighten the routine-day bar. This clarifies functioning tools, without reopening either walkway or preservation system.
asks.decision: Mature-colony workload and ordinary-job versus manual-order boundary.
asks.author: Codex Designer dry run, 2026-11-10
asks.speaker: agent
asks.review_status: Local evidence/wording check only; independent author review pending; not sent.

asks.title: Between the click and the blast
asks.picture: A shaft arms a trap while the good miner is elsewhere. A novice also has Mining enabled. The current code shows a countdown only when inspected and can send that novice to disarm automatically; failing its skill gate detonates it. The high-skill disarm rule itself is already settled.
asks.text: What should you be able to do between noticing the click and the explosion, and what would make losing that novice feel deserved?
asks.why: F1/F3. A real chance to react is different from a fuse that runs unnoticed while an automatic job makes the fatal choice.
asks.guess: I can stop the nearby work, get people clear, and send a suitable miner if one is close enough. A novice touching it should follow an informed choice, rather than a surprise automatic reassignment.
asks.tree_change: If the choice is local retreat, assert time and a readable cue for workers already there. If selecting a specialist is essential, require a deliberate or correctly gated assignment and demonstrate a nearby specialist reaching it. If automatic response is intended, require that its eligibility and lethal risk are clear before normal work assigns it. All branches preserve skilled disarm and failure detonation.
asks.decision: Player reaction window and responsibility for the disarm assignment.

asks.title: What a successful evacuation saves
asks.picture: The ordinary beast wakes after disturbance. People can walk away faster than it moves, but the dense station contains stores, beds and production. This is the station-eater, separate from the deliberately poured-solvent manhunter weapon. A day-ahead warning is already in its specification.
asks.text: When you call that evacuation a success, what has the colony carried away, and what has the tar taken back?
asks.why: F2/F3. Outwalking a slow pawn proves little if recovering anything useful is impossible, or if a giant's appetite can be satisfied by a few throwaway fixtures.
asks.guess: People and a chosen portion of valuable stores can escape; saving every building is not the bargain. I recommend a costly retreat with real choices, rather than a guaranteed loss or a cheap decoy solution.
asks.tree_change: People-only success sets a human survival scene and bounded warning. A meaningful salvage success adds hauling time, access and a limited useful recovery target. Relocation of most operations requires a longer preparation/recovery case. If a cheap decoy is an intended tactic, make that limit explicit; otherwise test it as a counterexample to station-eating. No answer reopens the beast's existence or the separate solvent weapon.
asks.decision: Useful evacuation outcome, appetite pacing and cheap-decoy rejection case.

asks.title: Yesterday's mouse-line after a belch
asks.picture: A belch has changed a route. Old tracks remain where workers remember walking; the new ground and plants have not yet settled. Later the mice and margins redraw. Honest mouse tells and slow living-map response are already required; their safe relationship during that interval is not spelled out.
asks.text: What should warn a careful returning worker's player that yesterday's route no longer tells the truth?
asks.why: F1. A living map can pass a plant-spawn test while its old signs actively mislead the player during the dangerous hours.
asks.guess: The fresh change in the ground is legible and old tracks cease to look like current evidence; new mouse behaviour becomes trustworthy as it appears. I would start with the ground and the animals themselves, consistent with the existing rule against a mouse-warning overlay.
asks.tree_change: If the new surface is sufficient, bind a read of an actual rewritten route with stale tracks still present. If old tracks must disappear or visibly age, require their transition and a control with an unchanged route. If the worker must wait for fresh mouse traffic, state that rule and demonstrate a practical way to distinguish old from new evidence. Any appearance choice needs a labelled mock or game exploration before a visual leaf is fixed.
asks.decision: Honesty of navigation signs during the rewrite-to-recovery interval.

asks.title: What makes another day's digging worth it
asks.picture: The colony has spent a day working the tar and has had to deal with a trap. Most current lottery finds are ordinary salvage; the preserved draw-joint is a real exception that teaches useful machinery. The ruled archive of older remains and machines has much more character than those placeholders.
asks.text: What single find would change tomorrow's plans enough to make that day's risk worthwhile?
asks.why: F2. A weighted table can work perfectly while the archive is merely a slow source of sellable junk. The prize must affect play, not just carry an ancient-sounding label.
asks.guess: A useful preserved mechanism that changes what I can build or safely attempt, with remains and lesser salvage making the dig feel like deep time. The draw-joint is a good concrete starting example.
asks.tree_change: A new practical tool requires a complete find-to-use scene, extending the existing learning model only as needed. Valuable material requires a meaningful production/trade decision. Historical discovery requires a recognisable reveal and a reason to care. A dangerous ancient machine adds a separately bounded wake/recovery scene. Whole prohibited ancient bodies and ordinary live-preserved fauna stay ruled out under every answer.
asks.decision: Archive reward that changes a colony decision, beyond generic currency.

asks.title: Two ways to put food under tar
asks.picture: A haul of food comes home. The shelf vault preserves the original and charges solvent to retrieve it; with Cold Storage installed, the vat instead makes sealed food that can age into pitch-aged food. Both systems are built, and bodies and hides also give the vault a wider job.
asks.text: What would make you put one haul in the vault and the next into sealed jars?
asks.why: F2/F3. These two built preservation systems arrived through different work. Their combined daily play needs a clear reason for choosing, without inventing a second solvent tax or making one a hidden trap.
asks.guess: The vault is flexible storage for food and other perishables I want back unchanged; the jars are deliberate food preparation, portable supplies and aging for a better ingredient. I recommend proving that distinction with ordinary cook and haul work.
asks.tree_change: If immediate flexible storage versus prepared/aged food is the choice, require both useful routes and an ordinary meal/hauling scene. If one is the emergency option, bind its access/time tradeoff. If there is a different distinction, derive only that contract. If the distinction does not matter, treat it as advisory while still covering both built systems; neither is offered for removal.
asks.decision: Combined purpose and ordinary-use contract of the two built preservation systems.
